topic.name: Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions Over General Curves

question.text: Evaluate the line integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = 3 \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathbf j$ and $C$ is the arc of the circle $x^2+y^2 = 16$ traversed from the point $A(4,0)$ to the point $B(0,4).$
question.explanation:
We will use the formula \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}. \]

So, along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 4\cos{t}, \qquad y = 4\sin{t}. \]

As a result,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= 3 \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathbf j \\[3pt] &= 3 \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{1}{4\cos{t}} \,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 4\cos{t} \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 4\sin{t} \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= \left( 3 \,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{1}{4\cos{t}} \,\mathbf{j} \right) \cdot \big( -4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &= 3\cdot (-4\sin{t}) + \dfrac{1}{4\cos{t}} \cdot 4\cos{t} \\[3pt] &= -12\sin{t} + 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2} ( -12\sin{t} + 1)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \Big[ 12\cos{t} + t \Big]_0^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \left(0 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - (12 + 0) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{2}-12 \end{align*}

example.title: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} - x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
question.explanation:
We will use the formula \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

So, along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \cos{t}, \qquad y = \sin{t}. \]

As a result,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= y\,\mathbf{i} - x\,\mathbf{j} \\[3pt] &= \sin{t} \,\mathbf{i} - \cos{t}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( \cos{t} \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( \sin{t} \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -\sin{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \cos{t}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= \big( \sin{t} \,\mathbf{i} - \cos{t}\,\mathbf{j}\big) \cdot \big( -\sin{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \cos{t}\,\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &=-\sin^2 t - \cos^2 t \\[5pt] &=-(\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t )\\[5pt] &=-1. \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} (-1)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\left.-t\right|_{0}^{2\pi}\\[5pt] &=-2\pi \end{align*}

example.title: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = x\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the curve $y =\sqrt{x^2+9}$ traversed from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(4,5).$
question.explanation:
We will use the formula \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) &= t\,\mathbf{i} + \sqrt{t^2+9}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 4. \end{align}

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t, \qquad y = \sqrt{t^2+9}. \]

As a result,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= t\,\mathbf{i} + \sqrt{t^2+9}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( \sqrt{t^2+9} \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+9}}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= \big( t\,\mathbf{i} + \sqrt{t^2+9}\,\mathbf{j} \big) \cdot \big( \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+9}}\,\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &= t \cdot 1 + \sqrt{t^2+9} \cdot \dfrac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+9}} \\[3pt] &= 2t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int_{0}^{4} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{4} 2t \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= t^2\Big|_0^4 \\[5pt] &=16 \end{align*}

question.text:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = x^2\,\mathbf{i} + \ln{y}\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the curve $y = e^{2x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,e^2)?$

Hint: Use the parametrization $\mathbf r(t) = t\,\mathbf i + e^{2t}\,\mathbf j.$
question.explanation:
We will use the formula \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) &= t\,\mathbf{i} + e^{2t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 1. \end{align}

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t, \qquad y = e^{2t}. \]

As a result,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= x^2\,\mathbf{i} + \ln{y}\,\mathbf{j} \\[3pt] &= t^2\,\mathbf{i} + \ln{e^{2t}}\,\mathbf{j}\\[3pt] &= t^2\,\mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( e^{2t} \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{i} + 2e^{2t}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= \big(t^2\,\mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j} \big) \cdot \big( \mathbf{i} + 2e^{2t}\,\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &= t^2 \cdot 1 + 2t \cdot 2e^{2t} \\[3pt] &= t^2 + 4te^{2t}. \end{align*}

Finally, we can write the integral as

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{1} t^2 + 4te^{2t} \,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{1} t(t + 4e^{2t}) \,\mathrm{d}t. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = -x\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
question.explanation:
We will use the formula \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t. \]

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

So, along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 4\cos{t}, \qquad y = 4\sin{t}. \]

As a result,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= x\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j} \\[3pt] &= -4\cos{t} \,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( -4\cos{t} \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 4\sin{t} \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= \big( -4\cos{t} \,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}\big) \cdot \big( -4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &=16\cos t\sin t + 16 \sin t\cos t \\[3pt] &=32\cos t\sin t \\[3pt] &=16\sin 2t. \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{2\pi} 16\sin 2t\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=-8\cos(2t)\Big|_{0}^{2\pi}\\[5pt] &=-8+8\\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}
